note: TED-Ed's 6-minute lesson on five Nobel laureates who tested their work on their own bodies, written by Shannon Odell, directed by Caitlin McCarthy (who also made video 56) and narrated by Addison Anderson. It opens on the smallest story: George de Hevesy, sure his boarding house is re-serving leftovers, sprinkles a radioactive tracer on his plate and catches it days later in the hash. Only then does it state its premise, and a stack of books with the names Forssmann, Theiler, Youyou and Warren & Marshall on their spines lays out what is coming. Everything is drawn in grainy ultramarine, lemon, coral and pink with glowing outlines, and organs get faces. Repetition is shown by multiplying the frame, passing days by suns and moons in a window, and Marshall's red tie opens into his stomach, then closes over it at the end of his story. The breakdown follows how five separate stories are fitted into one lesson, how each scene change grows out of a shape, and samples 41 moves as flip books.
transcript_kind: Creator captions, with each multi-line cue joined into one line

shot_notes.0: TED-Ed's logo on white, then 'Made in partnership with The Nobel Prize' in gold and 'Supported by' the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation. The only plain white frames in the film.
shot_notes.6: The film fades up from grey into night: George de Hevesy in bed under a slanted skylight of stars. The room, the bedding and the lamp are all one ultramarine, and only his face and arm are pink.
shot_notes.12: Indigestion as color: in two seconds his body flips to yellow, then red, as he tosses, and the camera starts to drop through the floor.
shot_notes.15: The kitchen below in cross-section, warm yellow wall over the blue floor. The landlady stirs a steaming pot while a stack of plates with leftover bones waits by the stove.
shot_notes.17: Close on the pot of hash, a bone poking out of it. The film's evidence, planted in the first ten seconds of the story.
shot_notes.19: A ladle tips the hash onto his plate from above his head, so the pot, the ladle and his worried face stack into one composition.
shot_notes.21: He points at the bone on his plate while the landlady glares over his shoulder: the accusation as a two-shot, no words needed.
shot_notes.23: She erupts. A red starburst flares behind her and the camera pulls back so he shrinks to half her size.
shot_notes.27: 'Who happened to be a trained chemist': he throws up gloved hands and his glasses go white. A second identity revealed by costume.
shot_notes.29: He holds up a vial that glows lemon yellow. Throughout the film, yellow with a soft halo marks whatever is active: tracer, vaccine, bacteria.
shot_notes.33: Overhead still life of his plate, fork, knife and napkin laid flat on blue. His hand shakes glowing powder over the leftovers.
shot_notes.36: The boarding house with suns and moons whirling past it on both sides: several days in two seconds.
shot_notes.39: A Geiger counter over the hash, yellow crackle lines bristling around the food. The proof is drawn as an outline, not a number.
shot_notes.43: Pull back to the whole dining table: every diner's plate crackles. One bad plate becomes a house of them.
shot_notes.47: '1913' in huge coral numerals on yellow, its last two digits rolling like an odometer toward the prize year.
shot_notes.51: '1943' has landed. De Hevesy steps in at the right holding a red box.
shot_notes.52: He opens the box on a gold medal, framed by sparkles. The prize is shown as an object, here and every time it returns.
shot_notes.55: Back at the kitchen sink, the counter now crackling over washed plates: the leftovers trick restated as a general method.
shot_notes.60: A red heart with a face, its arteries lit by moving yellow dots. 'Trace blood flow after a heart attack.'
shot_notes.64: The vessels tie themselves in a knot and deliver the dots to two worried kidneys. Drugs reaching their target, as a cartoon.
shot_notes.67: The blue tubes under the kidneys run on into a striped river through green hills: the watershed, drawn as the same line.
shot_notes.70: The premise as a lineup on blue: four self-experimenters, one crouching, a man in a ruff drinking from a flask, a woman in a lab coat tipping a vial at her head, and a man in a suit sitting on the floor.
shot_notes.76: The man in the suit has cut into his own leg. The lineup is the dark side of the premise, played as deadpan.
shot_notes.77: Hands covered in blisters: 'horrific infections'. The camera then tilts up the same body to its face.
shot_notes.80: 'Accidental psychedelic trips': the face floods with green, red and yellow, its eyes melting.
shot_notes.82: 'And even deaths': he falls back into a chalk outline on navy, with numbered evidence markers.
shot_notes.84: 'Great leaps in human understanding' taken literally: a tiny scientist on a stack of books, about to jump.
shot_notes.89: He hops across towers of books and lands by a glowing stack whose spines read FORSSMANN, THEILER, Youyou and WARREN & MARSHALL. The film's table of contents is a prop.
shot_notes.95: The Nobel medal, Alfred Nobel's profile engraved on gold, with the little scientist lounging on top.
shot_notes.99: Werner Forssmann, in a green graduation gown and mortarboard, sits for a portrait photographer.
shot_notes.104: His 'radical idea' is a raised finger and a red flash. The studio backdrop is about to be pulled away.
shot_notes.106: Behind the backdrop, a giant heart with a face, tiny masked figures perched on its vessels.
shot_notes.108: The procedure as a diagram: a dark blue body with a red heart and veins, a yellow tube about to enter from the right.
shot_notes.110: Close on the heart, eyebrows raised, beside the long looping vein the catheter will have to travel.
shot_notes.113: The yellow catheter threads up the arm to the heart, which settles into a satisfied face.
shot_notes.117: The diagram was on a blackboard. A lecture hall seen from behind the audience, Forssmann at the front.
shot_notes.119: Colleagues' hands shoot up in objection, a row of pointing fingers.
shot_notes.124: Forssmann at his desk at night, fingers steepled, deciding to do it himself.
shot_notes.127: A tube labelled 'Lidocaine' squeezed onto his bare yellow forearm, flat on blue.
shot_notes.129: His fingers feed the catheter into the vein at the elbow. The same framing holds for five seconds.
shot_notes.134: A sign reads 'X-RAY DEPT.' He walks down the stairs with the tube trailing from his arm.
shot_notes.135: He steps behind the screen and becomes a glowing skeleton with a red heart, the catheter running into it.
shot_notes.139: 'He repeated the procedure eight more times': the forearm multiplies across the frame until it is a wall of arms.
shot_notes.143: His arm vein used up, the catheter moves to his hairy thigh above a sock garter.
shot_notes.147: Forssmann in full color while his colleagues stand around him as translucent blue line drawings, hands raised in horror.
shot_notes.153: He hides his face, and the frame closes into a heart-shaped iris.
shot_notes.156: The heart cracks down the middle and falls apart in pieces: 'forced Forssmann to abandon cardiology'.
shot_notes.158: A wartime ward in green, Forssmann now a medical officer walking past the beds.
shot_notes.164: Home in 1945, in profile at a doorway, mouth open: the news is about to reach him.
shot_notes.170: A sunny cardiac ward, every patient with a heart on the monitor above the bed, all waving.
shot_notes.176: Forssmann close up, making a heart with his hands over the cheering ward.
shot_notes.179: André Cournand and Dickinson Richards in a tight two-shot, eyes sliding toward each other.
shot_notes.186: They demonstrate on a mannequin, half of it cut away to skeleton, in front of a chalkboard.
shot_notes.190: The scene shrinks into a coin, flips, and comes up Max Theiler, then flips again to Tu Youyou: two short stories announced in one move.
shot_notes.193: Hazard signs on blue: a body with a starburst inside, a skull, lightning, an exclamation mark, a dropper over a hand.
shot_notes.198: The body in the sign fills in as Theiler, the starburst now a yellow virus he holds like a crystal ball.
shot_notes.205: A yellow mosquito the size of his torso flies in, glowing like the virus.
shot_notes.206: Cut wide: tiny Theiler swats the mosquito in an empty field of blue. Scale as the joke.
shot_notes.211: The vaccine made in close-up: a dropper over a beaker of yellow liquid, his squinting eyes filling the top of the frame.
shot_notes.215: 'Many vaccine researchers did this': other researchers inject themselves, each on a solid field of green, yellow, pink or red.
shot_notes.219: One of them balloons into lumpy yellow and bursts into puffs. The risk, shown without blood.
shot_notes.224: Tu Youyou crouches inside a blood vessel, red cells drifting past and a spiky parasite approaching.
shot_notes.226: She holds up an infected red cell, dotted with parasites, close to her glasses.
shot_notes.231: A feverish patient in a hospital bed, face flushing red and fading back as the thermometer comes and goes: 'cycles of fever'.
shot_notes.236: The character 医 (medicine) fills the frame, the cover of an old medical text.
shot_notes.238: Youyou reading among towers of blue books, the research shown as a pile.
shot_notes.240: An open book labelled 'Sweet wormwood' with 青蒿素 (artemisinin) and the plant growing out of its pages.
shot_notes.241: The plant's stem becomes the line diagram of the artemisinin molecule, drawn inside a circle.
shot_notes.242: The parasite as a scowling blue ball with yellow limbs, gripping a red cell.
shot_notes.245: The pair shrink into a hole that turns out to be on a mouse's flank: 'animal trials'.
shot_notes.246: A lab with the mouse in a glass box, two colleagues in the foreground and Youyou raising her hand behind them.
shot_notes.252: She drinks the first dose straight from a test tube.
shot_notes.255: Thumbs up and a grin, her colleagues cheering on either side.
shot_notes.260: Barry Marshall in a lab coat and face shield, pointing ahead.
shot_notes.265: Marshall clutches his stomach under red jagged lines. 'Believed to be primarily caused by stress.'
shot_notes.267: His red tie peels away to show the stomach underneath, and the camera dives in.
shot_notes.277: Inside the stomach, its lining scalloped like a seam, small sores appear and a worried face forms in the middle of them.
shot_notes.280: Warren and Marshall at a lab bench with a microscope.
shot_notes.283: A yellow cloud of spiral bacteria billows out of the microscope eyepiece over them.
shot_notes.293: The stomach again, now crowded with yellow spirals.
shot_notes.295: Animal trials as a sulking pig with a stethoscope, the two scientists unimpressed.
shot_notes.300: Marshall raises a finger: 'took matters into his own...' and pats his belly: '...stomach.'
shot_notes.303: A healthy stomach with a smiling face and sparkles: his gut confirmed healthy.
shot_notes.305: Marshall holds up the scan of his own healthy gut.
shot_notes.307: The drink in thin white line on navy: a profile tipping back a tube, the yellow liquid the only solid shape.
shot_notes.312: The liquid fills the stomach and the bacteria inside it spell 'helicobacter pylori'.
shot_notes.314: Marshall in bed, Warren in a chair beside him, a window flipping between sun and moon. The same frame holds for ten days.
shot_notes.324: Antibiotics: a red and white capsule pushed into his mouth.
shot_notes.329: The capsule on a tongue, then a row of open mouths sliding across the frame: a treatment becoming standard.
shot_notes.333: The mouths close into lines that redraw as the stomach lining, a sore turning into a smiling face.
shot_notes.336: Untreated, the sores merge into a dark blob with yellow eyes: the cancer the narration warns of.
shot_notes.337: Hands pull back the intestine and it is his tie again: the film closes the gag it opened at 4:27.
shot_notes.341: 'Countless lives': a wallpaper of smiling figures with hearts on their chests.
shot_notes.346: All six laureates gathered on a blue hill, holding up gold medals.
shot_notes.350: Pull back: they stand on top of a stack of books.
shot_notes.355: The final tower: books, a microscope, a flask, a syringe and a globe, with tiny figures climbing it. It holds for 15 seconds.
shot_notes.368: Credits in a black band over the held navy: Shannon Odell, Caitlin McCarthy, Addison Anderson, and composer Salil Bhayani and sound designer Anthony Nguyen of cAMP Studio.

motion_intro: Caitlin McCarthy draws the film in a short list of colors, ultramarine and navy, lemon, coral, pink, mint and one green, with grain on every gradient and a soft glow along the outlines, so the whole film looks lit from behind like a screen. Characters are flat and rubbery, and camera moves step forward every eighth of a second, three frames at a time, which is why the cut detector counts 222 cuts. Many of them are the steps of one pan or push. Most scene changes grow out of something already in the frame: a studio backdrop pulled away, a heart-shaped iris that cracks, a coin that flips from one scientist to the next, a hazard sign whose silhouette fills in, a tie that opens into a stomach, a cell that turns out to be on a mouse. Repetition is shown by multiplying the frame (diners, arms, mouths), and time by a window that flips between sun and moon. The sequences below follow each story's key moves in order.

motion.title: Night, indigestion, and a drop into the kitchen
motion.text: The film fades up from grey at 6.25 to a blue bedroom: one man under a skylight of stars, the room, the bedding and the lamp all one ultramarine. He shifts at 9.0 and lies still for three seconds. From 12.0 his body flips yellow, then red, as he tosses, and from 12.75 the camera drops through the floor in steps about an eighth of a second apart, into a yellow kitchen where the landlady stirs a steaming pot beside a stack of used plates. At 15.5 it cuts to the pot itself.

motion.title: The landlady erupts
motion.text: He points at the bone on his plate while the landlady leans in over his shoulder, scowling. At 22.67 the camera jumps back and a red starburst flares behind her, so in one cut she doubles in size and he shrinks into his chair. She stays in that pose, hand on hip and a finger raised, with only small mouth moves, while the starburst holds behind her.

motion.title: Tracer on the leftovers, then the plate is taken
motion.text: He holds a glowing yellow vial up to his eye, and the film cuts to a flat overhead still life: plate, fork, knife and napkin laid out on blue. At 32.75 his hand enters from the top right and shakes the vial over the hash, flecks of yellow settling on it. At 35.0 another hand comes in from the top left and slides the plate out of frame, leaving the cutlery behind.

motion.title: Days pass around the boarding house, then a push into the window
motion.text: The boarding house stands still while two suns and two moons swing round it, swapping places every eighth of a second for about a second and a half. At 38.08 the camera pushes into one lit window, in steps, until its yellow pane fills the frame, and at 38.58 a plate of hash slides in on the yellow: days later, the same food.

motion.title: The counter crackles, then the whole table does
motion.text: A hand holds out the plate and de Hevesy lowers a Geiger counter over it. From 40.17 yellow zigzag lines bristle around the hash while he leans in. At 43.5 the camera pulls back to the whole long table, a dozen diners, every plate and the pot in the middle crackling with the same yellow lines.

motion.title: 1913 rolls to 1943
motion.text: Huge coral numerals drop in over the diners and fill the frame: '1913'. From 46.87 the last two digits roll vertically like an odometer, each at its own pace, through 1925, 1926, 1930 and 1942, and settle on '1943' at 48.87. The number holds for two seconds before de Hevesy slides in at the right with a red box, and he opens it on a gold medal at 52.0.

motion.title: From the sink to the heart to the kidneys
motion.text: Back at the sink, the counter crackles over the washed plates as the landlady takes them away. Her red back fills the frame, and the red becomes a heart: by 59.67 it has a face and four vessels running yellow dots. It grimaces, then opens its eyes and smiles at 1:01.33 as the dots flow. At 1:03.33 the vessels knot themselves together and carry the dots down to a pair of kidneys, who look alarmed.

motion.title: The kidneys' tubes become a river
motion.text: The kidneys, faces calming, hold for two seconds. From 1:06.5 the camera tilts down the two blue tubes under them, and by 1:07.0 the tubes have become one striped river running through green hills under a yellow sky. The heart, the kidneys and the watershed are drawn with the same rounded tube.

motion.title: Four self-experimenters, one with a knife
motion.text: Four figures on blue, posed like a class photo: one crouching, a man in a ruff, a woman in a lab coat, and a man in a suit sitting on the ground. Each does one small thing. The man in the ruff drinks from a flask and his eyes go red, the woman tips a vial against her head, and at 1:14.17 the man in the suit raises a cleaver and brings it down on his own leg, a spurt of red on the floor. None of them reacts.

motion.title: Blisters, a trip, and a chalk outline in one move
motion.text: Two clean hands fill the frame on a red jacket, and from 1:17.5 blisters swell up over them. At 1:19.25 the camera tilts up the same body to a calm face in glasses. From 1:20.25 its colors flood: green and red blotches spread from the eyes, the pupils go black, yellow drips down the nose. It snaps back at 1:21.75, the man tips backwards, and the camera pulls up and away until he is lying inside a red chalk outline with three evidence markers on navy. At 1:23.08 the same man springs up out of the outline and lands on a book.

motion.title: Leaps across book stacks to a table of contents
motion.text: A tiny scientist in a red jacket stands on a book, then at 1:24.33 the camera pulls back to show towers of books on green and he starts leaping between them like a platform game, panning right with him. At 1:29.0 a glowing stack slides into view, sparkles around it, its spines reading FORSSMANN, THEILER, Youyou and WARREN & MARSHALL. He waits on a nearby stack, then leaps onto it at 1:32.67 and the frame falls away to blue, where he lands on top of a Nobel medal.

motion.title: His idea pulls the backdrop away
motion.text: Forssmann, posing in his graduation gown, raises a finger and the photographer's flash bursts red behind the camera. At 1:45.38 the blue backdrop behind him is dragged off to the left like a curtain on a rail, a band of grain at its edge, and behind it is a giant red heart with a face and small masked figures perched on its vessels.

motion.title: The catheter route, drawn as a diagram
motion.text: A dark blue body sits on navy with a red heart and red veins. At 1:48.5 a yellow tube slides in from the right edge toward the elbow. The film cuts close to the heart beside a long looping vein, the heart frowning, then wide-eyed, then grimacing at 1:52.25 as the catheter makes its way along. Back on the body at 1:53.0, the vein from the arm to the heart has been threaded, and the heart relaxes into a smile.

motion.title: The diagram is on a blackboard, and the room objects
motion.text: The diagram is chalk on a blackboard, and at 1:56.33 the film cuts to the lecture hall from behind the audience, Forssmann at the front pointing at it. He folds his arms, and from 1:59.0 his colleagues' hands go up one after another, fingers pointing. At 2:01.0 it cuts to him alone at his desk.

motion.title: Anesthetic, then the catheter in the elbow
motion.text: At his desk he lowers his hands, and the film cuts to a bare yellow forearm flat on blue. A hand squeezes a tube labelled 'Lidocaine' onto the inside of the elbow, leaving a white daub, and leaves. At 2:08.0 his other hand brings the catheter in from below and feeds it into the vein in small pushes, the framing held still for three more seconds.

motion.title: Down the stairs to the X-ray screen
motion.text: A locked-off wide of a red stairwell, a sign reading 'X-RAY DEPT.' and a dark screen at the bottom. Forssmann walks down the stairs from the top left from 2:11.75, the catheter trailing from his arm, and at 2:14.75 steps behind the screen, which lights up as a white-line skeleton with a red heart, the yellow tube looping in from his arm.

motion.title: Eight more times: the arm multiplies
motion.text: The single forearm and catheter return, then from 2:17.5 a second copy slides in from the right, then a third, each with its own hand feeding a catheter. They keep arriving and squeezing closer until by 2:19.33 the frame is a wall of identical yellow arms, and from 2:21.5 a hairy thigh in green trousers swings in over them for the next attempt.

motion.title: The thigh, and back to the room
motion.text: Close on his thigh above a sock garter. His hand pushes the catheter in from 2:21.75 while one used forearm stays in the corner of the frame, its own hand still fiddling with the old catheter. At 2:27.0 the blue darkens and the shot dissolves into a wide of him on the chair, colleagues gathering around.

motion.title: Colleagues as ghosts around him
motion.text: Forssmann sits in full color on a chair, one leg out, while his colleagues surround him as translucent blue figures drawn only in pale line, hands up in horror. He waves them off, then sags and buries his face in his hands at 2:30.67. At 2:32.67 the edges of the frame close in.

motion.title: A heart-shaped iris cracks and falls apart
motion.text: The frame closes into a heart shape around him from 2:32.75 and shrinks to a small heart on navy by 2:33.88. It holds for about a second. A crack runs down its middle at 2:34.38, the two halves pull apart at 2:36.0, and the pieces fall away to reveal a wartime ward in green, Forssmann walking through it as a medical officer.

motion.title: Through the war ward to the door
motion.text: Forssmann marches left to right through a dim navy ward of soldiers in green, the camera panning with him past beds, nurses and bandaged soldiers. At 2:43.83 it cuts close as he lifts his cap at a doorway, and then holds on his profile.

motion.title: The cardiac ward cheers
motion.text: A locked-off pink ward with four beds, each patient under a monitor with a heart on it. Forssmann enters at the left, small hearts floating up from him, and walks to the beds as the patients wave. At 2:51.17 he throws both arms up in the foreground, filling half the frame, and the patients wave back.

motion.title: From his heart-hands to the two who proved it
motion.text: Forssmann rises into the foreground in close-up and makes a heart with his hands over the ward. At 2:58.25 a second face slides in from the right, a balding man with his chin in his hand, and Forssmann slides out: André Cournand and Dickinson Richards in a tight two-shot, eyes flicking toward each other for three seconds. At 3:02.75 they cut wide, standing either side of a mannequin in front of a chalkboard.

motion.title: A coin flips from one scientist to the next
motion.text: The mannequin demonstration shrinks into a blue disc on coral at 3:09.0 and turns on its vertical axis until it is a thin edge at 3:09.67. It turns back showing Max Theiler's face, holds for about half a second, turns edge-on at 3:11.08, and comes back as Tu Youyou. At 3:12.67 it turns once more, now a diamond, and opens into a hazard sign on magenta.

motion.title: The hazard sign fills in as Theiler
motion.text: A diamond warning sign with a dark silhouette and a yellow starburst sits in the middle as more signs slide in around it: a skull, lightning, an exclamation mark, a dropper over a hand. They slide out again from 3:16.0. At 3:16.83 the silhouette fills with color and becomes Theiler, the starburst now a yellow virus in his hands, and the diamond grows past the frame edges.

motion.title: A mosquito the size of a man, then a swat
motion.text: Theiler shrugs, then clutches his collar, worried. From 3:24.0 a yellow mosquito flies in from the right and grows until it is as big as his torso. He raises a fist. At 3:26.5 the film cuts very wide, Theiler tiny in an empty blue field, and he swats the mosquito, which drops to the ground with its legs up.

motion.title: Making the vaccine and injecting it
motion.text: Close on a beaker of clear liquid under Theiler's squinting eyes. A hand pours yellow in from above at 3:29.25 until the beaker is full, a dropper adds more, and from 3:31.75 a syringe draws the yellow up. At 3:33.75 the camera pulls back as he grips his shoulder and pushes the needle into his own arm.

motion.title: Other researchers, one color each
motion.text: Theiler holds his arm, then four other researchers inject themselves in the same pose, one after another, each on a flat field of a different color: green, yellow, pink, red. The last one swells into lumpy yellow from 3:38.5 and bursts into puffs of smoke at 3:41.17, and from the smoke Tu Youyou's face appears.

motion.title: Inside the bloodstream, then into the patient
motion.text: Tu Youyou crouches inside a blood vessel with wavy pink and yellow walls, red cells drifting past and a spiky red parasite approaching. She catches an infected cell at 3:45.25 and the film cuts to her holding it up to her glasses, dotted with yellow parasites. From 3:49.75 the camera pulls back fast, and the cell becomes a speck on a red surface, the flushed face of a fever patient.

motion.title: Cycles of fever
motion.text: A patient in a hospital bed with a heart monitor and a flower on the bedside table. A thermometer pops in and out of his mouth while his face and arms flush red, fade to pale, and flush again: two full cycles in four seconds. At 3:55.25 the frame cuts to the purple cover of a book.

motion.title: From an old medical text to a molecule
motion.text: The character 医 (medicine) fills the frame, and the camera pulls back to show it on the cover of a book, which Youyou is reading among towers of blue books. At 3:59.75 an open book labelled 'Sweet wormwood' and 青蒿素 (artemisinin) sprouts the plant, and at 4:00.5 the camera tilts up the stem into the line diagram of the artemisinin molecule in a circle. At 4:01.75 the molecule's circle becomes the round blue body of the parasite.

motion.title: The parasite lets go, and the scene is on a mouse
motion.text: The parasite, a blue ball with yellow arms and legs, grips a red cell, then lets go and waves its hands at 4:03.5, the cell smiling. The camera pulls back from 4:04.17 through red and blue flesh until the pair are in a small dark hole on the flank of a mouse at 4:05.33, which turns out to sit in a glass box on a lab bench, with Youyou behind it raising her hand.

motion.title: The first dose
motion.text: Youyou stands up behind the mouse cage. At 4:12.25 the film cuts to her face, eyes closed and smiling, and she drinks from a test tube. She holds still, eyes closed, for a full second and a half. At 4:14.5 she grins with two thumbs up, and the camera pulls back to two colleagues cheering, then gasping, either side of her.

motion.title: His tie opens into his stomach
motion.text: Marshall, in a pale blue shirt and red tie, gasps, then clutches his stomach as red jagged stress lines flare around his head. At 4:27.0 the camera pushes in and he lifts his tie aside. The tie opens like a flap, and by 4:27.88 the screen is his stomach, red inside a glowing yellow band, the first sore appearing in its wall.

motion.title: Bacteria billow out of the microscope
motion.text: The camera tilts down from the stomach to Warren and Marshall at a lab bench. At 4:42.5 a yellow cloud bursts out of the microscope and spreads over their heads, full of spiral bacteria. It holds for five seconds while the two of them stare up, then from 4:48.17 the cloud fills the frame, and at 4:51.83 it turns orange and becomes the inside of the stomach, crowded with yellow spirals.

motion.title: A pig, a pause, and 'his own... stomach'
motion.text: Warren and Marshall stand with arms crossed beside a pink pig with a stethoscope on its back. The pig sulks, flaps its trotters, and sulks again for four seconds. At 5:00.0 Marshall raises a finger, the music drops out, and he lowers it and pats his own belly. At 5:02.67 the film cuts to a smiling, sparkling healthy stomach.

motion.title: The drink, drawn in line, fills the stomach
motion.text: Marshall raises a glass. At 5:06.67 the film switches to thin white line on navy, his profile tipping back a tube, and the yellow liquid is the only solid shape. The camera follows the stream down through the throat into the stomach, which fills from the bottom up by 5:10.0. From 5:11.17 the bacteria inside rearrange into the words 'helicobacter pylori'. At 5:13.0 a yellow wipe brings in the bedroom.

motion.title: Ten days in one frame
motion.text: A locked-off bedroom: Marshall in bed, Warren reading in a chair beside him. The window flips between sun and moon every half second while Marshall goes from lying flat to sitting up holding his head, to sitting hunched over his stomach, to slumped back with his arms flung up, blue crack lines drawn on the sheets.

motion.title: A pill becomes a hundred mouths, and the mouths become a stomach
motion.text: Marshall pushes a red and white capsule into his mouth, grimaces, then relaxes into a smile on pink. At 5:27.5 his face drains of color and morphs into the capsule itself, which sits on a tongue in an open mouth at 5:28.5. More mouths slide in from both sides, each holding the pill, and close one by one into curved lines from 5:30.25. The lines redraw into a face at 5:33.0, a smiling sore in the stomach lining.

motion.title: The sore turns dark, and the tie closes
motion.text: The camera pans along the intestine past several sores. At 5:35.25 they merge into a dark blob with yellow eyes. At 5:37.25 yellow hands close the intestine like a shirt front, and the camera pulls back: it was Marshall's tie again, which he smooths down. He stands alone on green, then bends over and lifts something at 5:40.0 as a crowd rises into the frame.

motion.title: Countless lives, six medals, a stack of books
motion.text: A wallpaper of identical smiling figures, each with a heart on its chest, fills the frame and drifts upward. From 5:43.67 a yellow glow comes up at the bottom and the camera pans down under the crowd to Warren and Marshall holding up a medal on a blue hill. The other laureates step in around them from 5:45.67, each with a medal, and from 5:49.67 the camera pulls back to show they are standing on top of a stack of books, part of a tower that rises from 5:50.67.

lede: A TED-Ed lesson on five Nobel laureates who tested their discoveries on themselves: George de Hevesy, Werner Forssmann, Max Theiler, Tu Youyou and Barry Marshall, with his partner Robin Warren. Shannon Odell wrote it, Caitlin McCarthy directed and animated it, and Addison Anderson narrates over a score by cAMP Studio. It runs 6:16, with five and a half minutes of story.

It is worth studying for two things. First, how a list of five unrelated stories becomes one film: a cold open that tells the whole first story before the premise, a book stack that lays out what is coming, short and long stories in different shapes, and one image to close them all. Second, how flat 2D animation explains procedures nobody would want to film. Every step of a catheter, a vaccine or a stomach infection is drawn as a single clear action, organs get faces, repetition multiplies the frame, and almost every scene change grows out of a shape that is already on screen.

aspects.title: Five stories, three shapes
paragraphs: The lesson never opens with its premise. It opens on de Hevesy in bed with indigestion, and tells his whole story in under a minute: suspicion, accusation, a hidden test, proof, and the Nobel Prize thirty years later. Only at 1:09, after the anecdote has paid off, does the narrator say what the film is about. The viewer has already seen one example of the pattern, so the premise lands as a generalization rather than a promise.

Then the film shows its plan. The premise sequence ends on a glowing stack of books whose spines read FORSSMANN, THEILER, Youyou and WARREN & MARSHALL, a table of contents the viewer can read in the two seconds it holds. It is the only place the four remaining names appear together, and it means nobody has to wonder how long the lesson will run.

The remaining stories do not get equal time. Forssmann gets about 90 seconds and a full arc: idea, objection, the act, repetition, disgrace, war, and vindication by other people. Theiler and Youyou share one introduction ('Two other laureates also put their bodies on the line') and get about half a minute each, with no setback. Marshall gets nearly 90 seconds and is set up as the twist: the only one who experimented 'not to show something was safe, but to prove that it was dangerous'. Long, short, short, long keeps a list of five from feeling like a list.

Each story still runs on the same beats: a problem, someone refusing to help (the landlady, colleagues, failed animal trials), the self-dose, the proof, and the prize. The repetition is what lets the short stories be short. By Theiler the viewer knows the shape and only needs the details.

moments.text: The film starts with a man who can't sleep, not with its subject.
The table of contents on the spines.
Two stories announced in one coin flip.
Marshall's story starts with the old belief he will overturn.
All six laureates together, once, at the end.

aspects.title: A plain script with a few jokes
paragraphs: One narrator, Addison Anderson, carries every word. Nobody in the film speaks, so the characters act entirely in pantomime: the landlady's eruption, the colleagues' raised hands, Youyou's thumbs up. The narration states facts and the picture adds attitude, so the film can be funny without the script ever winking.

The few jokes in the script are timed for the picture. 'Marshall took matters into his own... stomach' leaves a gap where 'hands' should go, and the film fills it with Marshall raising a finger and the score dropping out, then a pat on the belly. 'Marshall's decision to trust his gut' comes as his tie closes and the crowd of saved lives rises, a pun the picture leaves alone. And 'not something just anyone should try at home' closes a film that has spent six minutes making self-experimentation look heroic.

Numbers are kept to a minimum. There are only a few years (1929, the 1930s, 1945, 1979, the 1940s) and two short counts ('eight more times', 'within five days' and 'after 10 days'). The one year the film puts on screen is 1943, rolled up from 1913 like an odometer, because the thirty-year wait for de Hevesy's prize is the point.

moments.text: 'Who happened to be a trained chemist': the reveal is in the costume.
The thirty years, counted on screen.
'His own...' and the pause.
'If left untreated, these ulcers can lead to cancer.'

aspects.title: Grainy color, glowing outlines, organs with faces
paragraphs: The look is a short list of saturated colors: ultramarine and navy for night, interiors and the inside of the body, lemon yellow, coral red, bubblegum pink, mint and one bottle green. Every gradient is grainy, and outlines carry a soft colored halo with a slight color fringe, as if the drawing were glowing on an old screen. It reads as warm and handmade even in the darkest scenes.

Color does a job. Lemon yellow with a glow marks whatever is active or dangerous: the radioactive tracer, the Geiger counter's crackle, the yellow fever virus and its mosquito, Theiler's vaccine, the cloud of H. pylori and Marshall's drink. Each laureate has fixed colors (Forssmann's yellow skin and green trousers, Theiler's pale blue skin and purple suit, Youyou's red skin and yellow jacket, Marshall's blue shirt and red tie), so they can be recognized from far away, inside a coin or in the final group shot. Forssmann's disgrace is shown in color against line: he stays in full color while his colleagues become pale blue outlines around him.

The body is drawn as characters. The heart has a face and changes expression as the catheter travels, kidneys look alarmed when the tracer arrives, the parasite is a blue ball with yellow arms, a stressed stomach grows a worried face, and Marshall's healthy gut smiles with sparkles. Procedures that would be hard to watch become readable and even funny, without losing what each step does.

There are no photographs, archival portraits or real places anywhere. The only words on screen are part of drawn objects: 'Lidocaine' on a tube, 'X-RAY DEPT.' on a sign, the names on book spines, 医 and 'Sweet wormwood' on book covers, and 'helicobacter pylori' spelled out by the bacteria themselves.

moments.text: Yellow wall, blue floor: the palette in one room.
Glowing yellow for anything active.
The heart as a character.
Color for him, pale outlines for everyone else.
The label written by the bacteria.

aspects.title: Scene changes that grow out of shapes
paragraphs: The film almost never just cuts from one idea to the next. A studio backdrop is pulled away to reveal a giant heart (1:45). Forssmann's disgrace closes into a heart-shaped iris that cracks and falls apart onto his wartime ward (2:33 to 2:36). The demonstration of the catheter shrinks into a coin that flips to Theiler, then to Youyou, then to a hazard sign (3:09 to 3:13). The hazard sign's silhouette fills in as Theiler, and its starburst becomes the virus in his hands. The sweet wormwood's stem becomes the line diagram of its molecule, and the molecule's circle becomes the parasite.

The camera travels through bodies and objects to change scale. It drops through the floor from bedroom to kitchen, tilts down the kidneys' tubes into a river, pulls back from an infected cell to the flushed face of a fever patient, pulls back from a parasite to a hole in a mouse, and dives into Marshall's stomach by lifting his tie, a move the film repeats at 5:37 to close his story. Each move tells the viewer that the next image is a closer or wider view of the same thing.

Repetition is shown by multiplying the frame. One plate that crackles becomes a table of crackling plates, one forearm becomes a wall of forearms for 'eight more times', and one mouth with a pill becomes a row of mouths when the antibiotic treatment becomes standard. Time passing is a window flipping between sun and moon, at the boarding house for 'days later' and over Marshall's bed for ten days, with the camera locked off so only the window and the patient change.

Camera moves advance in steps about an eighth of a second apart, so FFmpeg's cut detector finds 222 cuts, many of which are the steps of one pan or push. The real cutting is slower and often sits on a held composition: Cournand and Richards glance at each other for three seconds, Youyou holds still with her eyes closed after the dose, the final tower holds for fifteen.

aspects.title: A steady score that steps back for the big beats
paragraphs: cAMP Studio's score (composer Salil Bhayani, sound designer Anthony Nguyen) plays under almost every second of narration, mostly 7 to 15 dB under the voice. It is a bed, not a commentary, and the music's estimated tempo does not line up with the cuts any better than chance.

What matters is where it gets out of the way. The score thins as de Hevesy's story ends (about 1:04 to 1:11) and comes back as the premise begins. It drops out almost completely for about four seconds around 1:42, under Forssmann's 'radical idea', and returns as the backdrop is pulled away to show the heart. It sinks again from about 4:08 to 4:17, under Youyou's decision and dose, and comes back as the narration moves on to Marshall. And it disappears for two seconds at 5:00, so 'his own... stomach' lands in near silence.

The film ends the same way. The score stops under the last line, there is a second and a half of near silence around 5:55 over the held tower, and a short closing sting carries the credits. Demucs puts most of that sting in its voice stem, but recognition finds no words in it.

moments.text: The idea, in a gap in the music.
The dose, under a quieter score.
The pause before 'stomach'.
Near silence over the final tower.

aspects.title: Something to watch every second
paragraphs: A six-minute lesson about five people could easily sag in the middle, and this one keeps it moving in three ways. Each story has a small physical gag that has nothing to do with the facts: the landlady's starburst, the mosquito as big as Theiler before a wide shot shows him swatting it, the sulking pig with a stethoscope, the pill multiplying into a chorus of mouths. Each one is short, and none of them needs the narration.

Images also make the next line easy to predict. Lemon yellow keeps appearing, so the viewer learns to look for it. The window with the sun and moon returns when time passes, the medal returns when a prize is mentioned, and books return for study and knowledge. By the end, a stack of books and a gold medal tell the viewer what is coming before the narrator does.

And the film pays its own setups off. The tie that opened into Marshall's stomach closes again at the end of his story. The book stack from the premise becomes the base of the final tower. The six laureates, met one at a time, appear together only once, holding their medals in the last group shot, so the ending feels like the closing of the table of contents the film showed at 1:29.

moments.text: A gag that needs no words.
The scale joke.
The tie closes.
The book stack returns as the base.

patterns.name: Tell one whole story before the premise
patterns.text: Open on the most concrete, smallest example and finish it, prize and all, before saying what the film is about. The premise then lands as the lesson of something the viewer has just seen.

patterns.name: Put the table of contents in the world
patterns.text: Show what is coming as an object the characters live in, like names on book spines, held long enough to read. The viewer knows the length and order without a title card.

patterns.name: Vary the story lengths
patterns.text: In a list of stories, give the strongest two full arcs and compress the others into a shared introduction. Long, short, short, long keeps a list from feeling like a list.

patterns.name: Grow the next scene out of a shape
patterns.text: Change scenes through something already on screen: a backdrop pulled away, an iris that breaks, a coin that flips, a silhouette that fills in. Each change also says what the next scene has to do with this one.

patterns.name: Multiply the frame for repetition
patterns.text: When the narration says something happened many times, or to many people, duplicate the image across the frame instead of showing it again in sequence.

patterns.name: Give organs faces
patterns.text: Draw the body's parts as characters that react to the procedure. Each step becomes an expression, and a hard procedure becomes something people will watch.

patterns.name: Step back the music for the beat that matters
patterns.text: Keep the score steady under the voice, and pull it out for the decision, the dose or the joke. The silence marks the moment better than a sting would.

patterns.name: Close the gag you opened
patterns.text: Reuse a striking move at the end of a story, like the tie that opens into the stomach and later closes over it, so the story ends where it began.

craft.absent: There are no photographs, archival portraits, real places, maps, charts or on-screen captions naming people and dates, and nobody speaks except the narrator. Do not study it for collage or documentary evidence; study it for structuring several short biographies into one film, drawing medical procedures clearly, and changing scenes through shapes.
